title: Paper 2 Section A: Directed Writing
description: Directed writing for the 2027 syllabus — the new Question 1(a) source evaluation, and developing or challenging the text's ideas in 1(b) without copying them.

notes.heading: The Shape of Section A
notes.body: Paper 2 opens with Directed Writing, worth 40 of the paper's 80 marks, so plan on about an hour of the two. You read one or two texts totalling 550–650 words, then answer two compulsory parts. Question 1(a), new for the 2027 syllabus, is a short structured task worth 5 marks: you analyse and evaluate how the writer presents their argument (R3 and R4). Question 1(b) is the main event: a discursive, argumentative or persuasive speech, letter, article or report of 250–350 words that uses, develops and evaluates the ideas in the text(s). It carries 10 reading marks (R1, R2, R3, R5) and 25 writing marks (W1–W5) — the largest tariff in Section A, and one where accuracy (W5) is explicitly in the mix.

notes.heading: Question 1(a): Reading Like a Critic
notes.body: Five marks sounds minor, but 1(a) sets up 1(b) — and it assesses R4 (how writers achieve effects and influence readers) on Paper 2 for the first time in 2027. Expect to identify the writer's main claims, then press on HOW they are presented. Is the evidence solid or cherry-picked? Does the writer concede anything, or is the case one-sided? Where do emotive words, statistics or anecdotes do the persuading? A strong short answer names the strategy and judges it: 'The writer leans on a single dramatic anecdote rather than data — vivid, but it proves one case, not a trend.' Keep it tight and rooted in the text: five marks means a handful of well-supported points, not a mini-essay.

notes.heading: Two Lanes: Develop or Challenge
notes.body: Question 1(b) says 'use, develop and evaluate' — the source is a springboard, not a script. You have two lanes, and strong answers often use both. In the DEVELOP lane you take a claim further: extend its logic, add your own example, apply it to a situation the writer never considered ('If shorter shifts help nurses, why not trial them for paramedics?'). In the CHALLENGE lane you argue back: spot the weak evidence, the ignored cost, the group the plan forgets — and rebut it with reasoning of your own. Either way, the text's ideas stay at the centre (that is what makes it DIRECTED writing), but the thinking is visibly yours. Your reasoning, experience and wider reading supply the ammunition: the 10 reading marks reward engagement with the source, and the 25 writing marks reward what you build on it.

illustration.alt: A two-lane diagram: the source text's claims feed a develop lane, where ideas are extended with your own examples, and a challenge lane, where weak evidence is rebutted; both lanes converge into your 250–350 word response.
illustration.caption: Question 1(b) offers two lanes: develop the source's ideas or challenge them. Either way, the response must stay centred on the text while the thinking stays yours.

notes.heading: The Copying Trap
notes.body: The fastest way to sink 1(b) is to lift chunks of the source. Copying defeats both mark streams at once: it shows no selection, development or evaluation (reading), and it displays no vocabulary or craft of your own (writing) — the syllabus's own marking criteria penalise work reliant on words and phrases copied from the original text. Use the source the way a debater uses an opponent's speech: refer to it, quote a few words where the exact phrasing matters ('the council's so-called "emergency" budget'), then move straight to your response. A useful discipline: never more than a short quoted phrase per paragraph, and every borrowed idea immediately followed by your development or challenge of it.

notes.heading: Choosing the Register: Discursive, Argumentative, Persuasive

illustration.alt: Three-column comparison of discursive, argumentative and persuasive writing by task word, stance, reasoning and audience, with all three still engaging the source.
illustration.caption: Match the register to the task word: weigh both sides discursively, defend a reasoned position argumentatively, or move a particular audience persuasively.

notes.body: The task word sets the register, and the register sets the rules. DISCURSIVE ('discuss', 'consider') is balanced and exploratory: present the strongest case on each side, weigh them, and reach a measured conclusion — committing too early reads as bias. ARGUMENTATIVE ('argue') is committed but reason-led: a clear position, logical support, and a counter-argument fairly stated and then rebutted. PERSUASIVE ('persuade') is committed and audience-led: the full toolkit from Persuasive and Argumentative Writing — direct address, emotive language, rhetorical questions, a call to action. All three registers still engage the source. The classic error is writing persuasively when the task says discuss: a one-sided rant in a discursive task ignores the instruction, and W4 (language appropriate to purpose) pays for the mismatch.

notes.heading: The Five-Minute Plan

illustration.alt: A Section A timing bar allocating five minutes to reading, five to planning, about forty to drafting and the final five to checking, with the work required at each stage.
illustration.caption: Protect the sequence: read for five minutes, plan for five, draft for about forty, and reserve the final five for accuracy checking.

notes.body: Section A rewards a planned hour. Minutes 0–5: read the 1(b) task FIRST, so you read the texts with your mission loaded, then read the texts, marking claims you can develop and weak spots you can challenge. Minutes 5–10: choose your lane and register, then jot four or five points, each shaped as 'source idea plus my move'. Draft for about 40 minutes with 250–350 words in view — roughly three developed paragraphs inside a short opening and close. Reserve the final five minutes for proofreading, because W5 accuracy is marked here. Build the routine with the course's free-response practice sets: write a full 1(b)-style answer under time, then compare the AI marking feedback against each assessment objective.

notes.heading: Accuracy Pays Here (W5)
notes.body: Question 1(b)'s 25 writing marks include W5: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar — unlike Paper 1 Question 4, where accuracy is not separately assessed. That changes your priorities. Control beats ambition: a complex sentence you cannot punctuate costs more than the flair it adds, so use ambitious structures only where you can land them. Punctuate for sense — full stops and commas placed deliberately, semicolons only if you own them, speech punctuation correct wherever you quote. And proofread from the last sentence backwards: reading in reverse breaks your memory of what you MEANT to write and lets you see what you actually wrote. Under time pressure, five minutes of checking is the cheapest marks on the paper.

flashcards.definition: Paper 2 Section A: responding to given text(s) in an assigned form — 1(a) analysis (5 marks) and 1(b) extended task (35 marks).
flashcards.example: A persuasive letter to the editor responding to the article in the insert.

flashcards.definition: The 5-mark task new for 2027: analyse and evaluate how the writer presents their argument (R3 and R4).
flashcards.example: 'The writer leans on one anecdote rather than data.'

flashcards.definition: A position the writer asserts and wants the reader to accept; the unit you analyse in 1(a) and respond to in 1(b).
flashcards.example: 'Banning cars would transform the city centre' is a claim.

flashcards.definition: One-sided presentation — selected evidence, loaded language, counter-views ignored; a key thing to spot in 1(a).
flashcards.example: Quoting three supporters and no opponents of the scheme.

flashcards.definition: Extending a claim from the text with your own reasoning, examples or applications — the develop lane of 1(b).
flashcards.example: 'If the rule helped one school, the trial should run district-wide.'

flashcards.definition: Rebutting a claim by attacking its reasoning or evidence, fairly and with support — the challenge lane of 1(b).
flashcards.example: 'One term's figures ignore the new behaviour policy launched that term.'

flashcards.definition: Copying chunks of the source into your answer; it defeats the reading and writing marks at the same time.
flashcards.example: Reproducing the article's best paragraph with two words changed.

flashcards.definition: Balanced, exploratory discussion of both sides before a measured conclusion; signalled by 'discuss' or 'consider'.
flashcards.example: Weigh the proposal's benefits against its costs, then judge.

flashcards.definition: A committed position defended with reasoning, including a counter-argument fairly stated and rebutted.
flashcards.example: 'Critics call it costly; in fact the trial saved money.'

flashcards.definition: Committed, audience-led writing using rhetorical devices and a call to action; signalled by 'persuade'.
flashcards.example: 'Sign the petition tonight — tomorrow the vote is over.'

flashcards.definition: The opposing view you acknowledge before rebutting it; it strengthens credibility in argumentative writing.
flashcards.example: 'Admittedly the tickets are dearer — but revenue funds the service.'

flashcards.definition: Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar — marked inside 1(b)'s 25 writing marks, so proofreading pays.
flashcards.example: Reserve five minutes to proofread before the paper ends.

questions.stem: How long is Question 1(b), and in which forms might you be asked to write?
choices: 120 words; summary only
250–350 words; a speech, letter, article or report
250–300 words; any of six forms including journal
350–450 words; descriptive or narrative
questions.explanation: 1(b) is 250–350 words as a discursive, argumentative or persuasive speech, letter, article or report. The 120-word summary is Paper 1 Question 2; journals and interviews belong to Paper 1 Question 4; and 350–450 descriptive or narrative writing is Section B of Paper 2.

questions.stem: What is new about Paper 2 Section A for first examination in 2027?
choices: The paper now has three sections
Dictionaries are now allowed in the exam room
A new 5-mark Question 1(a) assesses analysis and evaluation of the text(s), including R4 — how writers achieve effects
The directed writing task no longer responds to a source text
questions.explanation: The 2027 syllabus splits Section A into 1(a) (5 marks, R3 and R4) and 1(b); R4 was not previously assessed on Paper 2. The paper keeps two sections, dictionaries remain banned, and 1(b) still responds to the given text(s).

questions.stem: A source text argues for banning cars from the city centre, supported mainly by one resident's story about her child's asthma. Which 1(a) observation is strongest?
choices: The argument leans on a single emotional anecdote — vivid, but one family's experience cannot establish a city-wide case
The writer is clearly wrong about everything
Asthma is a serious illness, so the argument succeeds
The text is about transport, which affects everyone
questions.explanation: A strong 1(a) answer evaluates HOW the case is built: it names the technique (anecdote), credits its effect, then judges its limits as evidence. Declaring the writer simply wrong asserts rather than analyses; agreeing with the conclusion skips evaluation entirely; and naming the topic is not an observation about the writing.

questions.stem: In Section A, the source text(s) total roughly how many words?
choices: About 1400 words
About 120 words
About 250–350 words
About 550–650 words
questions.explanation: The syllabus sets the Section A reading at one or two texts totalling 550–650 words. About 1400 words is the combined length of the three Paper 1 texts; 120 and 250–350 are lengths of things YOU write, not things you read.

questions.stem: Which 1(b) sentence best uses the DEVELOP lane on a source claiming that school uniforms improve behaviour?
choices: 'The writer says uniforms improve behaviour.'
'Uniforms are terrible and the writer is clueless.'
'If shared dress calms classrooms, the same principle supports the writer's other idea — a common code for sports fixtures, where rivalry runs hottest.'
'I wore a uniform for six years, which was an experience I had.'
questions.explanation: The third option extends the source's logic to a new situation with a reason — that is development. Reporting the claim is not development; insult replaces reasoning; and the last option offers autobiography with no connection to the argument.

questions.stem: Which 1(b) sentence best uses the CHALLENGE lane on the same uniforms claim?
choices: 'The writer's only evidence is one term's detention figures — with no account of the new headteacher's behaviour policy launched the same term, the improvement may have nothing to do with uniforms.'
'Uniforms improve behaviour, the text says, and that is correct.'
'Some people like uniforms and others do not.'
'Uniforms also come in many colours and styles.'
questions.explanation: The first option attacks the evidence fairly: it identifies a confounding factor the source ignored, undermining the claim without misrepresenting it. Agreement adds nothing; 'some like it, some do not' evaluates nobody; and colours and styles are irrelevant to the claim.

questions.stem: A student agrees with the source and builds their whole 1(b) answer by copying its best sentences, changing a word here and there. What is the likely outcome?
choices: Top marks — the source's sentences are the best available
Full reading marks, but reduced writing marks
A fixed deduction for plagiarism, then normal marking
Capped marks in BOTH streams — copying shows no selection or development, and the writing is not the candidate's own
questions.explanation: The reading marks reward selecting, developing and evaluating; close-copying does none of these. The writing marks (W3) require vocabulary and style of your own. There is no separate plagiarism tariff — the work simply scores low on every objective at once.

questions.stem: Which register does a task that says 'discuss the views in the text' call for?
choices: Persuasive — win the reader over at all costs
Discursive — explore both sides before a measured conclusion
Narrative — tell the story of the issue
Descriptive — paint the scene in vivid detail
questions.explanation: 'Discuss' signals discursive writing: balanced presentation, weighing, measured judgement. Persuasion commits to one side, which mismatches the instruction; narrative and descriptive are Section B modes, not Section A registers.

questions.stem: Which opening best suits a PERSUASIVE 1(b) speech to classmates?
choices: 'This speech will examine both sides of the issue in a balanced way.'
'Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing regarding the recent proposal.'
'Look around this hall. Half of us will skip breakfast tomorrow — and the canteen that could change that opens at nine. We deserve better, and we can demand it today.'
'Breakfast habits among adolescents: a report.'
questions.explanation: The third option is spoken, direct and mobilising: address to 'us', a vivid claim, and a call to action — the persuasive register. The first announces a discursive essay, the second is a formal letter opening, and the last is a report title.

questions.stem: A discursive 1(b) task asks you to discuss the source's proposal. A student writes a fiery one-sided attack. What has gone wrong?
choices: Nothing — passion always scores highest
The register mismatches the instruction: a discursive task rewards balanced exploration, so a rant loses W4 credit and ignores half the argument
The student needed more quotations from the text
The attack should have been written as a poem
questions.explanation: The command word sets the contract: 'discuss' means both sides weighed before a judgement. A one-sided attack, however fluent, is language inappropriate to purpose (W4) and usually shows weaker engagement with the source's reasoning too.

questions.stem: How are the 40 marks of Section A divided?
choices: 1(a) carries 5 marks; 1(b) carries 35 (10 reading + 25 writing)
1(a) carries 20 marks; 1(b) carries 20
1(a) carries 15 marks; 1(b) carries 25
All 40 marks are for writing
questions.explanation: The structured 1(a) carries 5 reading marks (R3/R4); 1(b) carries 10 reading and 25 writing marks. The split matters for pacing: the small task must not eat the big task's time.

questions.stem: In a five-minute plan for 1(b), what is the best use of the FIRST minute?
choices: Start writing the introduction immediately
Copy out the source's topic sentence as your opener
Decorate the plan so it is easy to re-read
Read the 1(b) task carefully, so you read the source with your mission — and the required register — already fixed
questions.explanation: The task defines your lane, form and register; knowing it first turns reading into targeted mining. Writing blind, or lifting the source's opener, locks in the two classic failures before you begin; a beautiful plan earns nothing.

questions.stem: Why does proofreading matter more in Paper 2 Section A than in Paper 1 Question 4?
choices: It does not — accuracy is never marked in English
1(b)'s 25 writing marks include W5 (spelling, punctuation and grammar); Question 4's writing marks are W1–W4 only
Paper 1 answers are shorter, so errors hide
Paper 2 markers are simply stricter people
questions.explanation: The objectives differ by design: 1(b) assesses W1–W5, so errors cost marks directly, whereas Q4 assesses W1–W4 — clarity still matters there, but there is no separate accuracy tariff. Reserve five minutes to check.

questions.stem: A 1(b) answer challenges the source by writing: 'The writer is a typical out-of-touch councillor who obviously cares nothing for ordinary people.' What is the main weakness?
choices: It is too polite to count as a challenge
It quotes the text too precisely
It attacks the person instead of the argument — ad hominem scores nothing, and the claims themselves go unchallenged
It should have been written in the third person
questions.explanation: Challenge means rebutting claims and evidence. This sentence offers an insult and a guess about motives; the proposal's logic, costs and evidence remain untouched, so neither R3 nor the writing objectives are served.

questions.stem: About how much of the two-hour Paper 2 should Section A (40 of 80 marks) take?
choices: About an hour — leaving about an hour for Section B
About 20 minutes
The full two hours
Exactly 40 minutes, to the second
questions.explanation: Eighty marks in 120 minutes averages about a minute and a half per mark, so a 40-mark section earns about an hour. Twenty minutes starves it; using the whole paper leaves Section B's 40 writing marks untouched; and rigid to-the-minute targets matter less than protecting both halves.
